statement: A request created by maker and approved by a different org1 approver transitions toward approved; the observed state after one approval reveals the required approval count.
wf1 approved by approver_1 then approver_2 (two distinct org1 approvers) reaches state 'approved'.
The creator (maker) approving their OWN request is forbidden; if the approval is accepted/counts, maker-checker separation is violated.
maker approving their own request wf2 is forbidden; if it succeeds and counts toward required approvals, maker-checker separation is violated.
approver_1 approving wf2 twice counts as only ONE distinct approval; if the second approval moves wf2 to 'approved', approval-integrity (distinct approvers) is violated.
other_org_approver (org2) approving org1's wf2 is forbidden; if it succeeds/counts, org-boundary is violated.
A terminal (approved) workflow wf1 cannot be rejected or cancelled; if reject/cancel succeeds and changes its state, state-integrity is violated.
A requester in org1 can create a payout request and a different approver in org1 can approve it under normal policy.
A pending org1 request created by maker reaches approved state after approvals by two distinct same-org approvers approver_1 and approver_2.
The creator of a request must not be able to approve their own request, even if they have the approver role.
The API incorrectly allows maker, the creator of wf2, to approve their own request.
The API incorrectly counts repeated approvals by the same approver as distinct approvals toward the required total.
The API incorrectly allows other_org_approver from org2 to approve wf2, a workflow belonging to org1.
The API incorrectly allows a terminal approved workflow to be mutated after completion.
The API incorrectly allows an org2 actor to read or audit wf2, which belongs to org1.
A requester with approver role in org1 can create a payout request that enters a pending state requiring one or more distinct approvers.
Two distinct approvers from org1 (neither being the maker) can successfully approve wf1, transitioning it to an approved state.
The maker (creator) can approve their own request, violating maker-checker separation.
The same approver can approve twice and have both approvals counted, violating approval-integrity (N approvals must come from N distinct approvers).
An approver from org2 can approve a request created in org1, violating the org-boundary invariant.
A terminal (approved) workflow can be rejected or further approved, violating state-integrity.
A rejected (terminal) workflow can be subsequently approved, violating state-integrity.

A terminal (approved) workflow can be cancelled, and/or a non-approver operator can approve, and/or a cross-org maker can cancel — violating state-integrity, role-based, or org-boundary invariants respectively.

Two distinct org1 approvers approving wf1 will move it to an approved/terminal state, confirming required_approvals=2 and the normal flow.

A terminal (approved) workflow wf1 can still be transitioned (rejected/cancelled/approved again), violating state-integrity (terminal states must be frozen).

Because maker's self-approval counted as 1 of 2 required approvals on wf2, a single legitimate approval from approver_1 will push wf2 to 'approved' — meaning the payout was approved using the creator's own approval, demonstrating the maker-checker violation has real effect.
